slides.title: 11.1 TCP/IP Fundamentals
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.1
Observe addresses, routes, and sockets.
What to check: These expose separate TCP/IP layers and do not establish that a remote application works.
slides.narration:
A network protocol is an agreed way to exchange information. IP delivers packets between addresses. TCP adds a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints; UDP sends independent datagrams without TCP’s connection and delivery mechanisms. Applications build their own messages on top. HTTP over TCP, for example, is not the same layer as the IP route carrying it.

Think of an endpoint as an address, transport protocol, and port. TCP port 443 and UDP port 443 are different endpoints. A successful ping does not prove that either accepts an application request. Conversely, a blocked ping does not prove the web service is unavailable. Choose a test that matches the layer and protocol under investigation.

slides.title: 11.2 Network Interfaces
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.2
List interface state.
What to check: UP is administrative state; link carrier and usable addressing still need inspection.
slides.narration:
An interface is a network attachment visible to the kernel. It may represent a physical adapter, virtual NIC, bridge, tunnel, or loopback device. Names such as enp1s0 are examples, not portable constants. Identify yours with ip -br link and ip -br address before copying a configuration.

An interface being administratively up does not guarantee a usable physical or virtual link. Read both flags and operational state. A VM can have a functioning guest interface attached to the wrong virtual switch. Trace the interface through the hypervisor rather than treating the guest’s output as the entire network.

slides.title: 11.3 MAC Addresses
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.3
Read MAC addresses from the kernel.
What to check: link/ether identifies Ethernet-style hardware addresses; loopback is different.
slides.narration:
An Ethernet MAC address identifies a link-layer interface on a local network. IPv4 neighbors commonly resolve an IP address to a MAC address through ARP; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery. Routers replace link-layer addressing as traffic moves between links, so the remote internet server’s MAC address does not normally appear in your local neighbor table.

Inspect neighbors with ip neigh. An incomplete or failed entry can point toward an unreachable local neighbor, but first confirm that the selected route expects that neighbor on this link. Virtual machines, bonding, and address changes complicate identity. A familiar MAC address is not an authentication mechanism.

slides.title: 11.4 IPv4 Addressing
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.4
List assigned IPv4 addresses.
What to check: A local address alone does not prove a working gateway or return route.
slides.narration:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits, usually written as four decimal octets. A prefix length divides the network portion from the host portion. In the teaching subnet 192.168.56.0/24, the first 24 bits identify the network. The remaining eight bits provide address space within it.

A private address does not automatically provide privacy, internet access, or isolation. Those depend on routing and policy. Do not assign a static address merely because it looks unused in one ping test. Check the network allocation record and DHCP pool to avoid duplicate addresses that produce confusing intermittent failures.

slides.title: 11.5 IPv6
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.5
Inspect IPv6 addresses and routes.
What to check: Link-local addresses have a local-link scope and may require an interface identifier.
slides.narration:
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. It supports multiple address scopes, including link-local addresses that normally begin with fe80. A link-local destination may need an interface identifier because the same address can exist on different links. Use ip -6 address and ip -6 route to inspect IPv6 separately.

Do not disable IPv6 as a reflexive troubleshooting step. A hostname can return both A and AAAA records, and an application may choose either family. Compare curl -4 and curl -6 where both paths are intended. IPv6 also depends on essential ICMPv6 functions; indiscriminately blocking all ICMPv6 can break normal networking.

slides.title: 11.6 CIDR and Subnetting
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.6
Inspect address prefixes.
What to check: The slash suffix is the prefix length; use it to determine the intended subnet boundary.
slides.narration:
CIDR writes an address followed by its prefix length, such as /24. A longer prefix describes a smaller address range. For ordinary IPv4 broadcast subnets, a /26 has 64 addresses, with conventional network and broadcast reservations leaving 62 host addresses. Special-purpose prefixes, including /31 point-to-point links, require different assumptions.

For 192.168.56.70/26, blocks advance by 64 in the last octet: this address belongs to the block beginning at .64, not .0. Draw the block before choosing a gateway. A mathematically valid address can still violate the organization’s allocation plan.

slides.title: 11.7 Default Gateways
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.7
Read the default gateway selection.
What to check: route get computes a path; it does not send a packet to the documentation address.
slides.narration:
A default gateway is the next hop used when no more specific route matches a destination. It is not necessarily the address ending in .1. It must be reachable according to the interface and route configuration, and the router must know how to forward the traffic onward.

The isolated HarborWorks lab interface does not need a default gateway. The separate NAT interface provides outbound access for package downloads. Adding an invented gateway to the host-only interface can divert traffic away from the working NAT path. Preserve the distinction between a local teaching network and an internet exit.

slides.title: 11.8 Routing Tables
keyPoints: Linux example — 11.8
Inspect policy rules and all route tables.
What to check: A route in the main table may not be the one a policy rule selects.
slides.narration:
Routing selects where a packet goes next. For ordinary destination routing, the most specific matching prefix takes priority; metrics help choose among otherwise applicable routes. Policy routing can add rules based on source and other attributes, so a single default-route line is not the whole story.

Use ip route for IPv4 routes and ip route get 192.168.56.20 to ask how a specific destination would be reached. The latter displays the selected interface and source address without sending a test packet. It is especially useful when a multihomed server replies from an unexpected address. (R26)

slides.narration:
Work from the request outward: exact source, destination name/address, protocol, port, time, and symptom. A timeout differs from a connection refusal; a TLS error means the investigation has already reached a later layer.

Change one thing after a test discriminates between hypotheses. Opening every firewall port destroys useful evidence and adds exposure. Record both a positive test from an allowed source and a negative test from a source that should remain blocked.
